What Happened?

Shares of computer processor maker Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) jumped 4.2% in the morning session after retreating Treasury yields and broad dip-buying following the previous week's technology sell-off lifted equities, as JPMorgan upgraded the chipmaker with an $85 price target.

The rebound follows a 4.5% drop in the Nasdaq the previous week, with sentiment stabilizing as the benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury yield pulled back to 5.085%, per CNBC reporting, easing valuation pressure across the semiconductor complex.

Separately, in research cited by TipRanks, JPMorgan analyst Harlan Sur upgraded Intel from Underweight, noting a more balanced risk-reward profile following a 36% decline in its share price from its June peak.Sur highlighted improving operational execution across client and data center processors alongside expanding opportunities in custom application-specific integrated circuits. The broker added that rising enterprise demand for agentic artificial intelligence workloads provides Intel with additional runway to stabilize its core processor footprint.

Is now the time to buy Intel? Access our full analysis report here, it's free.

What Is The Market Telling Us

Intel's shares are extremely volatile and have had 66 moves greater than 5% over the last year. In that context, today's move indicates the market considers this news meaningful but not something that would fundamentally change its perception of the business.

The previous big move we wrote about was 3 days ago when the stock dropped 4.5% on the news that investors weighed escalating borrowing costs and Federal Reserve remarks emphasizing price stability over rate cut signals.

Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh stressed that maintaining price stability remains the central bank's primary mandate, while deliberately avoiding signals regarding the future trajectory of interest rates following an earlier rate hike. The prospect of persistent higher borrowing costs creates significant friction for high-growth sectors, particularly artificial intelligence and semiconductor firms that require substantial capital expenditure to finance advanced chip design, research, and fabrication infrastructure. Higher interest rates also reduce the present value of projected long-term cash flows, prompting investors to reassess rich valuations across technology equities.

Consequently, market participants adopted a cautious stance, triggering broad-based downward pressure and heightened volatility throughout the chipmaking ecosystem as financing conditions tighten.

Tesla Rises on a Foundry Agreement With Intel as JPMorgan Upgrades the Stock ©CristianIS from pixabay and Matt Weissinger from Pexels via Canva
Key Takeaways

Intel shares rose [4%] today after JPMorgan upgraded the stock to Neutral from Underweight and kept its $85 price target.

Tesla committed to Intel's 14A process back in April, so the upgrade is today's news, and it rests on better execution and rising earnings estimates.

Intel's capital spending has been bigger than its cash from operations every year since 2022, so outside customers and its $20 billion stock sale are what pay for the foundry.

Intel reports third-quarter results on Oct. 29, the next chance to see new foundry customers and the dollars they commit.

Intel (INTC:NASDAQ) shares rose [4%] today after JPMorgan upgraded the stock to Neutral from Underweight. The bank had downgraded it in November 2022.

Tesla (TSLA:NASDAQ) shares also rose [3%] today. Much of today's coverage put the upgrade next to Tesla's deal to use Intel's 14A chipmaking process. That deal dates back to April, when Elon Musk told investors on Tesla's first-quarter call: "We plan to use Intel's 14A process, which is state-of-the-art."

Even so, the two stories belong together.

What JPMorgan sees

Analyst Harlan Sur pointed out that Intel is down about 36% from its June peak. The broader chip group fell 20% to 25% over the same stretch. He gives CEO Lip-Bu Tan credit, writing that "the team's execution on next-gen manufacturing has significantly improved."

He also thinks the estimates are too low:

"We believe increasing agentic AI workloads (CPU intensive) and a very tight supply chain for leading edge silicon should drive continued positive EPS revisions in the upcoming earnings season and through CY27."

JPMorgan's 2028 EPS estimate is about 15% above consensus.

It's still a cautious upgrade. Since JPMorgan's 2022 downgrade, Intel's share of server CPU revenue has fallen from 77% to 53%, and Sur expects a few more quarters of losses. Intel's outside foundry business brought in barely $1 billion of annualized revenue in the first half of 2026. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM:NYSE) brought in $150 billion.

Why the foundry needed Tesla

Tan had said that Intel could rethink its advanced foundry plans if it couldn't sign enough outside customers. Tesla's commitment took care of that.

The money was the other half of the problem. Intel's capital spending has been bigger than the cash its operations bring in every year since 2022.

Intel (INTC): cash from operations vs. capital expenditures, $ billions, fiscal 2021–2025 (TIKR)

Intel cut capex to $14.7 billion in 2025, and that was still about $5 billion more than its operations brought in. That's why Intel's $20 billion stock sale, set aside for new factories, matters. With an anchor customer and that cash, the multi-year plan looks fundable for the first time.
